The paper method: use it on every Read-it problem
    Roadmap: how to learn Python fast (Tech With Tim)

    Summary of "How I would learn Python programming FAST (If I could start over)" by Tech With Tim (13:36). Check off each step as you finish it. Your checks save in this browser.

    The one big idea

    Go deep, not wide. Learn the fundamentals, pick one area, and finish real projects in it. Jumping between topics is what wastes months.

    His mistakes (don't repeat them)

    • Learned everything at once: web dev, games, data science, scraping. Result: a mile wide, an inch deep.
    • Never finished anything. Started a project, got halfway, jumped to the next shiny thing.
    • After months, he couldn't build one full project in any area.
    • Fix: fundamentals first, then pick one direction. Specialization (going deep in one area) beats generalization (a little of everything), especially early.

    The 6-step path

    1. Non-negotiable. Don't touch any framework or library until these feel easy.

      TopicWhat it coversIn this trainer?
      Variables, data typesstrings, numbers (int/float), booleans (True/False)Levels 1–4
      Control flowif / else, for loops, while loopsLevels 5–10
      Functionsdef, parameters (names in the def line), arguments (values you pass in), return valuesLevels 11–14
      Data structureslists, dictionaries, tuples, sets, and when to use each. Dictionaries show up everywhere.Lists and tuples: Levels 15–25 · Dictionaries and sets: Levels 26–31
      List comprehensionsa one-line way to build a list, like [x * 2 for x in nums]. Very Python-specific, very useful.Level 23
      File I/Oreading and writing files (I/O = input/output)Next up
      Error handlingtry / except / finally: catch an error instead of crashingNext up

      Goal: write a 100–200 line program from scratch without looking up syntax every 30 seconds. You don't need to memorize everything.

      Practice projects: reverse a list · a number-guessing game · a choose-your-own-adventure game. Doable in 2–4 weeks if you code every day and don't rush.

    2. OOP = organizing code into classes (blueprints) and objects (things built from the blueprint). This is the biggest gap for self-taught devs. You can get far without it, but you'll hit a ceiling fast.

      • Classes and objects
      • __init__: the initialization method. Runs when you create an object and sets it up.
      • Attributes: variables that belong to an object (like account.balance).
      • Inheritance: a class that borrows everything from another class, then adds its own stuff.
      • Dunder methods ("double underscore"): __str__, __repr__, __len__. They control how Python does things like printing, len(), +, and indexing on your objects.
      • Judgment: know when something should be a class vs. a plain function vs. just a variable.

      Why it matters: once OOP clicks, you understand how Python works under the hood.

    3. How to organize code across many files and manage what your project depends on.

      • import statements: pull code from another file or library.
      • if __name__ == "__main__": means "only run this part when this file is run directly, not when it's imported."
      • pip: the tool that installs packages (code other people wrote).
      • Virtual environment (venv): a separate box of packages for each project, so projects don't clash.
      • Built-in modules to try: random, os, json.
      • Read docs for a package you've never used, and use code you've never seen in a tutorial.
      • Practice: split one 500-line script into a few clean files. Learn dependencies (packages your project needs) and environment variables (settings like API keys stored outside your code).

      Around 5:29 there's a sponsored segment for DataCamp's Python Fundamentals track. His point: a structured track in the right order beats random tutorials. Optional. Your class plus this trainer already give you that order.

    4. He calls this the most important step, and the one he got most wrong.

      DirectionTools
      Web developmentDjango, Flask, FastAPI
      Data science / MLNumPy, pandas, scikit-learn, PyTorch
      Automation / scriptingfile handling, APIs, web scraping
      Backend / APIsFastAPI
      Games (for practice)Pygame
      • What "deep" means: you can build full projects from scratch, you know the common patterns, and you could interview on it.
      • Web dev: build 3–4 complete web apps, not one tutorial.
      • Data science: do 5–6 end-to-end analyses on real data sets.
      • Resist branching out early. Being good at one thing is what makes you hirable.
      • Build things slightly above your level. Not way above, or you'll get discouraged.
      • Tutorial rule: use a tutorial to learn a concept, then immediately build something similar without it. That's where the real learning happens.
      • Finish everything. One finished project teaches more than five half-done ones.
      • Bugs and problems force you to think, look up syntax, and find the right module. That struggle is the point.
      • Idea source: search "top 5 Python projects for [your direction]" and build them.
      • Put everything on GitHub: it's a backup, and it becomes your portfolio for jobs.

      21 projects mapped to your course

    6. Not glamorous, but these separate hobbyists from pros.

      SkillWhat to do
      Read other people's codeOpen-source projects on GitHub, and the source of modules you use. Compare their code to yours side by side.
      Use a debuggerA debugger pauses your code and lets you step through it line by line. Print statements work, but this saves hours. Learn it early. (The stepper in this trainer is the same idea.)
      Write testsA test is code that checks your code gives the right answer. Start with pytest. He says you can learn it in about 30 minutes. He skipped this for years and regretted it.
      Learn Git properlyBeyond the basic 4–5 commands: merge conflicts, rolling back to old commits, checking history, working with a team.
      Get comfy in the terminalChange folders, make folders, delete files, run a file. Matters more now with AI tools that run in the command line.

    His honest take

    • Python is easy to start, hard to get good at. Fundamentals take weeks, real skill takes months to years.
    • He has close to 20,000 hours of coding and still doesn't call himself an expert.
    • Demand for Python devs, especially in AI and data science, is the highest it's been. The time pays off.
    • The path in one line: fundamentals → OOP → organize code → pick a direction → go deep with projects → no shortcuts.
    • Once you're strong in one niche, other skills come naturally, and you're already employable.
    Where you are right now

    Levels 1–31 here cover most of Step 1: all of Ch 7 (lists, tuples, list comprehensions) and Ch 9 (dictionaries and sets). Still to go in Step 1: file I/O and try/except. For Step 4, your AI engineer / FDE goal points to APIs and automation or data science / ML. Pick one when you get there.
